{{< include _elements-kit.qmd >}}

A **style** or **genre** is recognised by its features: the instruments, the harmony, the rhythm, the textures it likes.
Naming the style is only half the answer. Say *which features* told you.

## 1. Western classical music

| | **Baroque** (about 1600–1750) | **Classical** (about 1750–1820) | **Romantic** (about 1800–1910) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Composers | Bach, Vivaldi, Handel | Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven | Schubert, Chopin, Wagner, late Beethoven |
| Instruments | harpsichord, small orchestra (mostly strings), **basso continuo** | the **piano** replaces the harpsichord; the orchestra grows (clarinets, horns) | a large orchestra, more brass and percussion; piano music for virtuosos |
| Dynamics | **terraced** (sudden loud/quiet) | a wider range, crescendos | a huge range, constant change |
| Melody | long, decorated with **ornaments** | balanced, regular phrases (4 + 4 [measures]{.nn}); elegant | long, expressive; the **leitmotif** |
| Harmony | major and minor keys settled in | simple, clear chords; **Alberti bass** | **chromatic** chords, unusual key changes |
| Texture | often **polyphonic** (counterpoint) | mostly **melody and accompaniment** | rich and full |
| Tempo | steady | steady | **rubato** (pushing and pulling the tempo) |

The periods overlap. Beethoven is the usual bridge between Classical and Romantic.

## 2. Jazz and blues

- **Swung rhythm**: pairs of [eighth notes]{.nn} played long-short ([Reading Swing](reading-swing.qmd)).
- **Blue notes**: the 3rd, 5th and 7th of the scale bent down, by anything from a quarter tone to a [half step]{.nn}.
- The **12-bar blues** chord pattern ([Blues Changes](blues-changes.qmd)).
- **Extended chords**: 7ths, 9ths and more.
- **Improvisation**: players make up their parts as they perform.
- A **rhythm section** (drums, double bass, piano or guitar) and a **front line** (saxophones, trumpets, trombones).
- **Walking bass**: a steady line of [quarter notes]{.nn} walking up and down through the chords.

## 3. Musical theatre

A story told through music, singing, acting and dance.

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Overture** | the music before the show begins, usually built from its main tunes |
| **Solo / duet / chorus number** | a song for one character, two characters, or the whole company |
| **Recitative** | speech-like singing that moves the story on, in shows that are all sung |
| Kinds of show | book musicals (songs between spoken scenes), **sung-through** (no speaking), **jukebox** (built from existing hit songs), film-to-stage |

Composers: Leonard Bernstein (*West Side Story*), Stephen Sondheim, Andrew Lloyd Webber, Lin-Manuel Miranda.

## 4. Film music

Film music supports what is on screen. Ask how each feature fits the scene:

| Scene | Features you might hear |
|---|---|
| Car chase | fast tempo, loud, driving ostinato, sudden changes |
| War film | military snare drum, brass fanfares; a lone instrument (monophonic) for isolation |
| Horror | dissonant chords, a repeated pattern building tension, sudden loud stabs |
| Romance | strings, legato melody, rich harmony, rubato |

A **leitmotif** is a short idea tied to a character or thing that returns whenever it appears. Composers: John Williams,
Hans Zimmer, Howard Shore, Jerry Goldsmith.

## 5. Pop and rock

**Pop** is commercial music written to appeal to lots of people. **Rock** is usually harder and louder, built on guitars
and drums, though it includes rock ballads. Both are mostly in verse–chorus [form](elements-structure.qmd#popular-song-forms),
often with a **riff**, a repeated pattern that makes a song memorable.

| Section | What it does |
|---|---|
| Intro | sets the mood, often instruments only |
| Verse | tells the story: same tune, new words each time |
| Chorus | the main message: same tune and words each time |
| Bridge / middle 8 | a contrasting section, often 8 [measures]{.nn} |
| Outro | finishes the song |

## 6. Minimalism

From the 1960s, mostly in the USA. Composers: Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Terry Riley, John Adams.

- Built on **repetition** of short patterns.
- The patterns change **gradually**, one note or one beat at a time.
- **Slow-changing harmony**, often one chord for a long time.
- Layers that drift in and out of line with each other (*phasing*).

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="140"><script type="text/plain">

T:One cell, growing a note at a time
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
c e g e c e g e|c e g a c e g a|c e g a b e g a|c e g a b d' g a|]
</script></div>

**For students**

"Alberti bass." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberti_bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberti_bass). Lowest, highest, middle, highest; Classical era; Mozart K. 545.

"Basso continuo." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basso_continuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basso_continuo). Chord instruments (harpsichord, organ, lute, theorbo…) and bass instruments (cello, double bass, bass viol, bassoon); figured bass.

"Blue note." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_note). Lowered 3rd, 5th and 7th; between a quarter tone and a semitone.

"Classical period (music)." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_period_(music)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_period_(music)). Classical roughly 1750–1820; Baroque c. 1600–1750; Romantic c. 1800–1910; melody over a subordinate accompaniment such as an Alberti bass.

"Minimal music." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music). US West Coast, late 1950s–early 1960s; Young, Riley, Reich, Glass, Adams; repetition, phase shifting, additive process, consonant harmony.
